Comparison with Rust > SLA vs Rust vs Go Performance Measurements (native / WASM / compilation / networking)

SLA vs Rust vs Go Performance Measurements (native / WASM / compilation / networking)

This page is the full comparison re-measured on 2026-10-24 on the slarust project (the previous snapshot was 2026-10-22): 10 core loads + hello, the two output chains native and WASM, cold/hot compilation, output size, peak memory, optimization levels, and compilation scalability. All SLA/Rust programs produce item-by-item identical checksums, so the multiples below are implementation differences for the same algorithm, not load differences. This round of re-measurement includes the cold/hot start fixes merged on 2026-10-24 (the SLA plugin content-hash freshness gate + SA parallel CGU branch cache write-back), and the hot-compilation conclusions have completely reversed.

NoteThis page is a reproducible measured snapshot, not a permanent conclusion. The toolchain is the sla plugin master (2026-10-24, including the cold/hot start fixes) / SA 0.1.8 (sci 346f68b9), Rust 1.99.1, Go 1.27.3, Wasmtime 25.0.2, on Linux x86_64 (AMD EPYC 7B12, 8 vCPU, 50GB memory). The “Optimization levels and variants” section was not re-measured in this round and is still 2026-10-22 data, as noted in that section.

One-Sentence Conclusion

On the current version, Rust release's native/WASM runtime medians are about 1.43× / 1.43× faster than SLA respectively (excluding the matmul outlier). The compilation conclusions have completely reversed this round: for cold compilation of conventional projects Rust is still faster (taking 0.42× (native) / 0.53× (WASM) of SLA's time), but for hot compilation SLA is now level with Rust (native geometric mean Rust/SLA ≈ 1.02), and for WASM hot compilation SLA is instead about 2.24× faster — rebuilds with unchanged content are now short-circuited as a whole by the freshness gate and no longer fully recompiled. SLA's WASM output size, after stripping DWARF, is about 1/6 of Rust's on typical loads and only about 1/10 in the optimal framing, but matmul is instead about 1.2×; native size is still about 28×. SLA network throughput now exceeds Go across the board, and at c=256 it is about 3.3× faster than after the fix in the previous version.

Summary

  • Correctness: the SLA/Rust checksums of all 11 programs (10 core loads + hello) are identical.
  • Native: excluding hello/matmul, Rust is 1.43× faster in geometric mean; including matmul it is 1.97× faster. SLA is still 1.35× faster on sort; hashmap is basically level this round (Rust slightly faster, 0.92×).
  • WASM: excluding hello/matmul, Rust is 1.43× faster; including matmul it is 1.93× faster. SLA's mandelbrot advantage in the previous version (1.87×) has disappeared this round, with the two sides level; the loopsum gap has narrowed from 3.2× to 1.17×.
  • Compilation: for conventional source code, Rust cold compilation takes about 0.42× (native) / 0.53× (WASM) of SLA's time; for hot compilation (touch without changing content) SLA is level with Rust (native), and about 2.24× faster for WASM. matmul native cold compilation is an outlier: SLA needs 13.5s (70.1s in the previous version), Rust 0.13s.
  • Size-optimal: native SLA about 8,910KB vs Rust about 276KB (about 32× larger); WASM typical SLA 1.8–4.8KB vs Rust 31.8–34.3KB (about 10× smaller; matmul is an exception, SLA is about 1.65× larger).
  • Memory: in large-array scenarios SLA RSS is 2–20× higher (sieve 422MB vs 21MB, bytes 528MB vs 35MB).
  • Default optimization (2026-10-22 data, not re-measured this round): SLA's default build is roughly at the Rust debug level (sieve/bytes 3–9× slower), and the matmul/sort default builds segfault; you must use --release-fast.
  • Network concurrency: with 4 independent processes and 1 listener per process, SLA is 31k–182k rps, now exceeding Go across the board (13.8k–113k); Rust is 36k–378k (1.2–2.7× faster). SLA's RSS is stable throughout at about 19–21MB, with no per-request growth.

Measurement Framing

The source code is in benchmarks/sla/*.sla and benchmarks/rust/src/bin/*.rs. SLA uses build-exe/build-wasm --release-fast; Rust uses cargo build --release (opt-level=3, lto=false, codegen-units=16, panic=abort) and wasm32-wasip1. Cold compilation deletes SLA's .sa_cache/.sla-cache and adds --no-incremental, while Rust uses a fresh CARGO_TARGET_DIR; hot compilation keeps the caches and touches both sides' source files (content unchanged) before rebuilding — under this framing SLA hits the content-hash freshness gate (see the “Hot compilation” section). Runtime is the median of 7 runs (native) / 5 runs (WASM), timing includes process startup, and WASM uses Wasmtime 25.0.2.

Key limitations: single-threaded; SLA currently reads 0 after pushing to a Vec<f64>, so both sides use a fixed [f64; 4096] array for matmul; SLA has no syntax for exporting WASM functions and can only run as a _start command; Node 20.19's WASI makes both SLA and Rust trigger a V8 trap when some large-memory modules exit, so WASM data uniformly uses Wasmtime.

Before measurement, both sides' source files are touched (content unchanged). Rust release does not enable incremental by default and recompiles the whole crate. This round's conclusion is completely reversed from the previous version: on native the two sides' geometric means are basically level (Rust/SLA ≈ 1.02, and SLA is instead faster on larger sources such as sort/hashmap/sieve), while on the WASM side SLA is uniformly about 2.24× faster, and SLA's hot-compilation times for all loads converge to the same order of magnitude (native about 94–108ms, WASM about 46–68ms), independent of source size — this is the signature of a cache short-circuit hit.

Fix on 2026-10-24: zero changes no longer trigger a full recompilation. The previous version's measured conclusion that “SLA has no Cargo-style short-circuit and build-exe still rewrites the executable” has been replaced by two fixes: (1) The SLA plugin adds a whole-compilation freshness gate — it stores a Wyhash manifest of the dependency closure file by file in .sla-cache/fresh/, and a rebuild with unchanged content skips the whole frontend and reuses the existing output (can be disabled with SLA_NO_FRESHNESS_CACHE=1); (2) SA's parallel CGU branch (explicit --jobs with ≥100 functions) previously never wrote back to .sa_cache, and the plugin used to append --jobs auto by default to delegated SA commands; the two together meant large projects' caches could never be built, and both are now fixed. Separately measured: a 288-module project with zero changes went from about 0.70s to about 0.05s for sla build-exe; a comment-only change reruns the frontend but the SA cache still hits and the output is byte-identical.

On the SLA side, --release-fast is used (the --release-small output is the same) and .debug*/name are removed; on the Rust side, profile.size is used (opt-level="z", LTO, codegen-units=1, panic="abort", strip="symbols") and the WASM debug sections are then removed. Network Concurrency (HTTP/1.1 keep-alive)

Responses are uniformly 200 OK, text/plain, body ok. SLA uses the http-server plugin with 4 independent processes (18092–18095), each with 1 listener + 1 SLA accept worker, setting TCP_NODELAY after accept; Rust is 4 processes of thread-per-connection; Go is 4 net/http processes. The client polls the 4 ports round-robin by connection, with 20,000 requests per level, 2 repetitions taking the median, restarting the server at each level.

1617,235182,415338,81699,2260.07/0.13/0.1619954
6411,899167,657377,740113,2300.35/0.49/0.81201056
2565,919123,872340,513105,5401.95/2.10/2.34211260
  • Re-measured on 2026-10-24: SLA exceeds Go at all concurrency levels (Go/SLA is 0.44×/0.54×/0.68×/0.85×); the gap to Rust has narrowed to 1.2×/1.9×/2.3×/2.7× (c=1/16/64/256). Compared with after the fix on 2026-10-22 (21–24k / 111–137k / 86–90k / 35–40k), SLA improves again this round by about 1.4×/1.5×/1.9×/3.3×, with the most obvious improvement at high concurrency (4 processes combined, 20,000 requests per level, 2 runs taking the median, errors=0).
  • The RSS leak remains fixed: before the fix, SLA grew by about 56KB per request, reaching about 1.1GB at c=1 and about 3.6GB at c=256 after 20k requests; this round SLA's RSS is about 19–21MB throughout, with no growth with the number of requests. See the root cause below for the reason.
  • The deployment topology determines throughput (2026-10-22 conclusion, re-measured this round with the same topology): the same plugin driven by C, with a single listener + 1 worker, was originally about 3.1k, adding TCP_NODELAY after accept raised it to about 7.4k; 4-thread serve_threaded was about 4.1k; 4 listeners × 4 threads instead dropped to 2.3–2.7k. Putting 4 listeners in the same SLA process gives only 8–12k; they must be split into 4 independent processes.
  • Plugin fix (2026-10-22): the SA host's exported pthread_join(int32_t,uint8_t*) shadowed the libc version, causing serve_threaded's std.Thread.join to return immediately; it has been changed to detach + an atomic completion counter. SLA closure function pointers must take the code from the vtable and cannot pass PTR_BYTE_ADD(handle,0).
  • Build: this SLA program still needs the two steps sla build + sa build-exe (this round all four servers built successfully in one go, including the newly installed http-server plugin).

Conclusions and Recommendations

  1. Runtime: SLA is about 1.4× slower than Rust release on most loads (geometric mean, the same for native/WASM); the matmul gap is 35.7×. SLA's advantage is concentrated in unordered indexed access (sort, overtaking on both native and WASM), possibly related to the generated code omitting bounds checks (not confirmed by disassembly); hashmap is level with Rust this round.
  2. WASM: the overall gap is close to native; fib/nbody/mandelbrot are level with Rust, and the loopsum gap has narrowed substantially. SLA's mandelbrot advantage in the previous version did not recur this round and is no longer a conclusion.
  3. Compilation: SLA cold compilation is still slow (Rust takes 0.42×/0.53× of its time); hot compilation has reversed — rebuilds with unchanged content are short-circuited as a whole by the freshness gate, level with Rust on native and about 2.24× faster on WASM, and the “zero-change full recompilation” problem is closed. matmul native cold compilation at 13.5s (70.1s in the previous version) is still the primary fix target, and the LLVM optimization explosion of --release-fast on fixed arrays + nested loops should continue to be investigated; matmul WASM cold compilation rose back to 2.36s this round and also awaits investigation.
  4. Size: in the size-optimal configuration, native is still clearly larger for SLA (about 8.9MB vs Rust about 0.28MB, about 32×). For WASM, with both sides in their optimal configurations, SLA is about 10× smaller on typical loads, but matmul is instead about 1.65× larger; when reporting size you must note the build configuration and whether it was stripped.
  5. Memory: fix the reclamation of old blocks and the capacity policy when Vec grows; the 15–20× RSS gap on sieve/bytes will limit edge deployment.
  6. Default build (2026-10-22 data): the default optimization level is roughly at the Rust debug level (some loads 3–9× slower), and matmul/sort crash; the documentation should explicitly require --release-fast, and the default code generation for aggregate types should be fixed.
  7. Networking: SLA throughput steps up again this round (182k at c=16, 168k at c=64, 124k at c=256), now exceeding Go across the board, with the gap to Rust narrowed to 1.2–2.7×; the roughly 56KB-per-request RSS leak was fixed long ago (see the root cause), and RSS is stable throughout this round. The remaining gap is mainly latency at high concurrency (c=256 SLA p50 1.95ms vs Rust 0.43ms), and the next step should investigate shared-pool lock contention in multi-worker accept.
  8. Follow-up: the numeric/WASM part only covers single-threaded loads; networking only covers HTTP/1.1 keep-alive. async, FFI, package management, etc. need separate benchmarks.

Root Cause

Fix 1 — Symbol binding: sci/src/runtime/sa_std.zig adds .visibility = .hidden to mmap/munmap/signal/dlopen/dlsym/dlclose/pthread_join/sqlite3_*. Plugins no longer bind to no-op stub functions in the host that do nothing.

Fix 2 — Allocator: sa_plugin_http_server's HttpServer.init changes from page_allocator to c_allocator, so each request no longer needs to execute one mmap and one munmap; the WebSocket frame buffer is replaced in sync as well.

Verification: running LD_DEBUG=bindings, libhttp-server.so's munmap/mmap64/mremap/pthread_join/malloc all bind to libc; nm -D --defined-only confirms that neither sa nor the server exports these symbols anymore; the tests pthread-vtable-smoke, sa-std-unit, plugin-host-smoke and the plugin's zig build test (17 pass / 1 skip) all pass.

Reproduction

npm install -g @slalang/sla
rustup target add wasm32-wasip1
curl -L -o /tmp/wasmtime.tar.xz \
  https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/releases/download/v25.0.2/wasmtime-v25.0.2-x86_64-linux.tar.xz
tar -xf /tmp/wasmtime.tar.xz -C /tmp
cd slarust
python3 scripts/bench.py --mode all --runs 7
python3 scripts/analyze.py > results/analysis.md
python3 scripts/render_report.py
cd benchmarks/net
bash build.sh
python3 run_bench.py --servers sla,rust,go --concurrency 1,16,64,256 --requests 20000
python3 summarize.py
